name: Great Smoky Mountains
blurb: Mast-rich hardwood forests, salamanders and bears under threat from tiny pests.

tip.title: Fail the acorn crop
tip.text: Oak mast fuels bears, turkeys, deer and squirrels. Cut Oaks & hickories and see the animals that depend on autumn nuts, and the predators above them, feel it.

notes: The story and why it matters come from the Wikipedia articles listed below (Great Smoky Mountains National Park, American black bear, Brook trout). A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.desc: Once a major canopy tree, it was killed off by chestnut blight in the early to mid 1900s. Sprouts still grow but rarely reach the canopy.
A dominant cove tree that shades cool streams and damp ground. The hemlock woolly adelgid, which sucks sap from the tree, is killing hemlocks across the southern Appalachians.
Browses plants and eats acorns. The NPS lists bobcats and coyotes among the predators that help keep deer numbers in check.
Eats and caches acorns and nuts. Bears are known to raid squirrel nut caches.
Forages on the forest floor for acorns, fruits and insects.
The park's largest mammal. Overhunting removed it, and it was reintroduced in 2001, now seen mostly in Cataloochee and Oconaluftee. Grazes grass and other plants.

nodes.name: American black bear
nodes.desc: About 1,900 bears live in the park. Mostly plant eaters, they switch from fruit in summer to hard mast in autumn, and also take insects, trout, carrion and fawns.
The only wild cat left in the park. Preys on deer and smaller animals such as squirrels and turkeys.
Arrived in the late 1900s and is now the park's largest wild canine, filling the role left after the failed red wolf reintroduction of 1991.
Powers the leafy summer canopy and the understory below it.
Rich, moist soil in the coves and slopes supports the tall hardwood forest.

nodes.name: Fungi & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down fallen leaves, logs and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.

link_ideas.what: Red wolves removed from the Smokies in 1998 were moved to Alligator River

story: Great Smoky Mountains National Park covers 2,114 km² across Tennessee and North Carolina. Oaks feed deer, squirrels, turkeys and black bears. Bears also eat berries and deer, and bobcats hunt deer.
matters: It is one of the largest protected areas in the eastern United States. About 1,500 black bears live here, roughly two per square mile.
